en-e1-l1.title: Alphabet and First Sounds
en-e1-l1.concept: Words dey easy to remember when you know their first sound and first letter. Follow along and pronounce dem.

en-e1-l2.title: Greetings
en-e1-l2.concept: When you meet somebody, say **Hello**; when you dey go, say **Goodbye**. Tell your name with **My name is ...**.

en-e1-l3.title: Numbers and Colours
en-e1-l3.concept: Learn number words like one, two, three... and colour words like red, blue, yellow...

en-e1-l4.title: Family
en-e1-l4.concept: Words for family members include mother, father, grandmother, and baby.

en-e1-l5.title: Classroom Words
en-e1-l5.concept: Try to say classroom words like desk, chair, bag, pencil, book... in English.

en-e2-l1.title: Names of Animals and Things
en-e2-l1.concept: A word wey name something, like rabbit, bird, or fish, na **noun**.

en-e2-l2.title: Words for Actions
en-e2-l2.concept: A word wey show action, like jump, run, or eat, na **verb**.

en-e2-l3.concept: **I like ...** mean “I like ...”; **I have ...** mean “I get ...”.

en-e2-l4.title: Making Short Sentences
en-e2-l4.concept: Use **am** after I, and **are** after You. Sentence order na “who → how/wetin dem do”.

en-e2-l5.title: Reading Short Texts
en-e2-l5.concept: When you dey read, first find di words from di question inside di text.

en-e3-abc1.title: Uppercase and Lowercase Letters
en-e3-abc1.concept: Alphabet get **uppercase** and **lowercase** letters. Many pairs look different, so learn dem one pair at a time. Pay special attention to letters wey look alike, like b, d, p, q.

en-e3-l1.title: Making Sentences
en-e3-l1.concept: Sentence order na “who → do wetin → what”. Add **-s** to di verb after He, She, or a person name.

en-e3-l2.title: Pronouns
en-e3-l2.concept: Instead of names, you fit use **He**, **She**, **It**, **They**, and **We**.

en-e3-l3.title: Present and Past Tense
en-e3-l3.concept: Use **present tense** for things happening now or regularly. For past events, add **-ed** to di end of di verb to make **past tense**.

en-e3-l4.title: Daily Routine
en-e3-l4.concept: Learn how to say your daily routine in English: get up, brush my teeth, eat breakfast, go to bed...

en-e3-l5.title: Understanding a Text
en-e3-l5.concept: Read di text and find who did something, when dem do am, and wetin dem do.

en-e3-snd1.title: Relationship between sounds and letters
en-e3-snd1.concept: Di first sound and first letter of a word dey connected. Learn di connection by finding words wey start with di same sound. Sometimes two letters like ph make di f sound.

en-e4-l1.title: Present, past, and future
en-e4-l1.concept: Use **present tense** for now or things wey happen often, **-ed** for past things, and **will + base verb** for things wey go happen.

en-e4-l2.title: Questions and negative sentences
en-e4-l2.concept: Start questions with **Do/Does**. To say no, use **don't/doesn't**.

en-e4-l3.title: Words for appearance and feelings
en-e4-l3.concept: Words like big, small, hot, and cold describe how something look or feel.

en-e4-l4.title: Words for places
en-e4-l4.concept: Use **on**, **in**, **under**, and **behind** to tell where things dey.

en-e4-l5.title: Reading short passages
en-e4-l5.concept: Find and answer who, where, and what somebody do in di passage.

en-e5-l1.title: Articles, plural forms, and There is/are
en-e5-l1.concept: Use **an** before a vowel sound and **a** before a consonant sound. Use **There is** for one thing and **There are** for more than one.

en-e5-l2.title: Comparing things
en-e5-l2.concept: To compare two things, use **-er + than**. For di most of something, use **the -est**. Use **more** with long words.

en-e5-l3.title: Talking about the future
en-e5-l3.concept: Talk about future things with **will + base verb** or **be going to + base verb**.

en-e5-l4.title: Rewriting sentences
en-e5-l4.concept: Put **not / don't / doesn't / didn't** in negative sentences. Start questions with **Are / Do / Does**.

en-e5-l5.title: Understanding passages
en-e5-l5.concept: When you read a long passage, look for who, where, when, and what, like you dey underline dem.

en-e6-l1.title: Review of tenses
en-e6-l1.concept: Use **be + -ing** for things happening now, **past tense** for past things, and **will / be going to** for future things.

en-e6-l2.concept: After **can**, **must**, **should**, and **may**, use di base form of di verb.

en-e6-l3.title: Building vocabulary
en-e6-l3.concept: Learn words with similar meanings and opposite meanings together to double your vocabulary.

en-e6-l4.title: Connecting words
en-e6-l4.concept: Connect sentences with **because** for a reason, **so** for a result, **but** for contrast, **if** for a condition, and **when** for a time.

en-e6-l5.title: Reading paragraphs
en-e6-l5.concept: Read passages with several sentences and find who did what, when, and why.

en-e6-pun1.title: Capital letters and punctuation
en-e6-pun1.concept: Start each sentence with a **capital letter** and end am with di correct **punctuation mark**. Usually, statements end with a full stop (.), questions with a question mark (?), and surprise or strong feelings with an exclamation mark (!). Always capitalize people names and I.

en-e6-seq1.title: Understanding the order of events
en-e6-seq1.concept: Look for order words like **First**, **Then / Next**, **After that**, and **Finally** to know di order wey things happen.

en-h1-l1.title: Perfect tense and perfect continuous
en-h1-l1.concept: Had + p.p. talk about something wey happen before another past event; have been -ing describe an action wey continue up to now.

en-h1-l2.title: Relative Adverbs and Noun Clauses
en-h1-l2.concept: Where, when, and why be relative words wey work as adverbs; whether and that dey start noun clauses.

en-h1-l3.title: Participial Phrases
en-h1-l3.concept: Remove di conjunction and subject, then change di verb to -ing. Di implied subject must be di same.

en-h1-l4.title: Linking Words and How Ideas Flow
en-h1-l4.concept: Know di difference between cause and result (so, therefore), contrast (however), example (for example), and addition (in addition).

en-h1-l5.title: Finding Main Ideas and Inferring Missing Words
en-h1-l5.concept: The main idea often dey after However, where a common belief turn around, or for di final sentence. Infer missing words from di flow: problem → solution → result.

en-h2-l1.title: Inversion and Emphasis
en-h2-l1.concept: When Never, Hardly, or Only then come first in a sentence, use auxiliary verb + subject order. Use It is ~ that for emphasis.

en-h2-l2.title: Conditionals
en-h2-l2.concept: For I wish, as if, and If clauses, use past tense for things contrary to now; use had p.p. for things contrary to the past.

en-h2-l3.title: Compound Relatives and Concession Clauses
en-h2-l3.concept: Whatever, whoever, whichever, and however + adjective mean “any ...” or “no matter how ...”.

en-h2-l4.title: Words in Context
en-h2-l4.concept: Use clues from contrast, examples, and causes, plus prefixes, to figure out unfamiliar word meanings.

en-h2-l5.title: How a Text Builds Its Argument
en-h2-l5.concept: Follow di text using references and linking words, then gather details to identify di conclusion.
en-h2-l5.example: In this way = by doing like this

en-h3-l1.title: Parallel Structure and Subject-Verb Agreement
en-h3-l1.concept: Phrases joined by and, but, or should have matching forms; make di verb agree with di main subject.

en-h3-l2.title: Mood, Tone, and Purpose
en-h3-l2.concept: Use description and emotion words to identify di mood; identify di purpose from whether di text dey request, guide, or persuade.
en-h3-l2.example: Please store enough water. → giving advice

en-h3-l3.title: Sentence Order and Insertion
en-h3-l3.concept: Use linking words, references, and time order to arrange sentences and find where a given sentence fit.

en-h3-l4.title: Collocations and Idioms
en-h3-l4.concept: Learn word pairs wey often dey used together, like make a decision, take a risk, heavy rain; use di situation to infer idiom meanings.
en-h3-l4.example: the last straw = di final thing wey person fit tolerate

en-h3-l5.title: Completing a Summary
en-h3-l5.concept: Find di main ideas and contrast expressions in a text, then shorten dem to one sentence.

en-h3e-l1.title: Choosing What to Say in Each Situation
en-h3e-l1.concept: For conversation questions, check whether di grammar correct and whether di way of speaking natural and polite for dat situation. Common topics include making suggestions, interrupting, replying to praise, idioms, and indirect speech.

en-h3e-l2.title: Workplace Expressions and Collocations
en-h3e-l2.concept: Workplace English focus on idioms (touch base), abbreviations (ASAP and others), and verb-preposition pairs (collocations). No translate word by word; remember di phrases as people use dem at work.

en-h3e-l3.title: Reading Information Critically
en-h3e-l3.concept: For media English, e important to tell facts from opinions and judge whether reasoning behind a claim make sense. Remember terms like image descriptions (alt text, caption) and editing tools by their purpose.

en-h3e-l4.title: Cultural vocabulary and an open attitude
en-h3e-l4.concept: For topics about world cultures, learn key words such as culture, diversity, and stereotype, along with phrases for understanding other cultures without judging them. Distinguish similar-looking words using context clues.

en-h3e-l5.title: Reading literature with literary terms
en-h3e-l5.concept: Literature questions focus on knowing each term’s definition and applying it to a scene in a story. Distinguish foreshadowing, symbolism, point of view, theme, and character roles.

en-h3e-l6.title: Identifying arguments and fallacies
en-h3e-l6.concept: In a debate, you need to distinguish terms (such as motion and rebuttal), types of evidence, and logical fallacies. When evaluating a claim, first ask, “What evidence supports this?”

en-h3e-l7.title: Writing clearly for a purpose
en-h3e-l7.concept: Choose a format that fits the purpose and audience, and check sentence structure (subject and verb) and the logic of linking words. In specific writing such as a résumé, concrete actions and numbers are better than vague claims.

en-l1.title: Learning everyday words
en-l1.concept: Common words are easier to remember when you learn their **sound + meaning + spelling** together. Tap the speaker button to hear the pronunciation.
en-l1.example: library = library / desk = desk / milk = milk

en-l2.title: The be verbs am / are / is
en-l2.concept: The form of the be verb changes with the subject: **I → am**, **he / she / it → is**, **you / we / they → are**.

en-l3.title: Simple present verbs
en-l3.concept: When the subject is **he / she / it (third-person singular)**, add **-s / -es** to the verb. Add -es to verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -s, -x, or -o; for a consonant + y, change y to i and add -es!

en-l4.title: Plural forms and making sentences
en-l4.concept: For more than one noun, usually add **-s**; add **-es** to nouns ending in -x, and memorize irregular plurals separately. Sentence order is **subject → verb → the rest**.

en-m2-l1.title: Present perfect
en-m2-l1.concept: Have/has + past participle. It expresses experience, completion, or continuation. Distinguish since (a point in time) from for (a duration).

en-m2-l2.title: Passive voice
en-m2-l2.concept: Use be + past participle to show that something is done or happens to someone. Add the agent with by.

en-m2-l3.title: Infinitives and gerunds
en-m2-l3.concept: Want, hope, and decide take an infinitive; enjoy, finish, and avoid take a gerund. Stop + to V expresses purpose; stop + V-ing means to quit an action.

en-m2-l4.title: Comparatives and superlatives
en-m2-l4.concept: Use -er/-est or more/most. Use than with a comparative and the with a superlative. Good → better → best is irregular.

en-m2-l5.title: Reading: main idea and details
en-m2-l5.concept: Read the question first and find the sentence with the clue. A title and main idea cover the passage as a whole.
en-m2-l5.example: As a result = as a result

en-m2-sum1.title: Summarizing a passage
en-m2-sum1.concept: To summarize a passage, identify the **main idea** and shorten it to one or two sentences. A sentence that gives only one detail, adds information absent from the passage, or is too broad is not a good summary.

en-m3-l1.title: Relative pronouns
en-m3-l1.concept: Join two sentences using who (people), which (things), that (either), or whose (possession).

en-m3-l2.title: Conditionals and the past subjunctive
en-m3-l2.concept: If + present, will + verb (a possible event). If + past, would + verb (a hypothetical situation contrary to the present).

en-m3-l3.title: Embedded questions
en-m3-l3.concept: Use question word + subject + verb order. Do not use do/does/did.

en-m3-l4.title: Participles
en-m3-l4.concept: -ing mean active/action still dey happen, while -ed mean passive or finished. For feelings, use -ing for the thing wey cause the feeling, and -ed for the person wey feel am.

en-m3-l5.title: Reading: Inference and Writer’s Purpose
en-m3-l5.concept: Join the clues to make an inference, and decide the writer’s purpose by checking requests and claims.
en-m3-l5.example: Could you tell me ...? → question (request for information)

Think wetin people go hope for after war don end, then find the word for that state.

e-h3e-lit-3.explanation: Correct answer na omniscient point of view. The narrator know the thoughts of several characters. Limited point of view only tells the thoughts of one character, so e no match the example wey show the inner thoughts of two people.
hints: For point-of-view question, check who dey talk and how many people's thoughts the narrator know.
Check whether the example narrate the thoughts of both Anna and Tom, then choose the point of view wey fit that range.

e-h3e-lit-4.explanation: Correct answer na Kindness often comes back to those who give it. E turn the cause and effect in the story into a general idea about life. The story takes place in a market only describe the setting; e no be the theme.
hints: The theme na the general idea the story dey express about life, no be the plot or setting.
Check whether one sentence generalize the link between the boy action and the result, and whether e avoid saying the opposite of the story.

e-h3e-lit-5.explanation: Correct answer na protagonist. Na the central character wey get a goal and move the story forward. Antagonist dey oppose the protagonist, so na the opposite role.
hints: Character terms dey differ by role: the central character, the person opposing them, and the narrator no be the same.
Compare the description wants something and drives the action with the definitions of each option.

e-h3e-lit-d1.explanation: A regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables na rhythm (meter). Plot structure na the order of events, so e no concern sound.
hints: Put the definition stressed and unstressed syllables, regular pattern into one sentence using your own words, then choose the matching option.
If stressed and unstressed syllables alternate, what kind of feeling do you hear? Find the term for that feeling.

e-h3e-media-1.explanation: Correct answer na to describe an image for people wey no fit see am. Alt text tells them wetin dey in the image through a screen reader or when the image no load. Copy protection na the work of another technology.
hints: Break down the term. Alt na short form of alternative.
Think who this feature helps and in what situation; cross out options wey no connect to its purpose.

e-h3e-media-2.explanation: Correct answer na The new park is the most beautiful place in town. The claim say it is the most beautiful na opinion because people fit disagree. The opening month, area, and number of playgrounds na facts wey person fit check.
hints: Facts fit be checked, but opinions differ from person to person. Check whether each sentence can be verified.
Look whether the sentence gives checkable details like dates, area, or number, or contains an evaluative phrase.

e-h3e-media-3.explanation: Correct answer na say e dey assume say tea cause the person to get better. Say the person feel better after drinking tea no mean say na the tea cause am. Formal style na only writing style; e no be weakness for the reasoning.
hints: Summarize in one line how this advert move from the evidence to the conclusion. Then ask yourself whether the evidence alone support that conclusion well. Check whether the option dey talk about the reasoning link or only how the writing look.
Focus on how dem connect drinking tea with getting better to reach the conclusion; remove options wey only talk about word choice or writing style.

e-h3e-media-4.explanation: Correct answer na Students gather with balloons at the annual school fair. The students, balloons, and school event all match wetin the photo show. An option about a runner crossing the finish line alone no match the photo at all.
hints: Caption suppose describe the people, place, and action wey really dey inside the photo.
First write down the people, place, and objects for the scene wey the question show, then compare how each option match dem.

e-h3e-media-5.explanation: Correct answer na Track changes. E dey show proposed edits without deleting the original text. Print preview only show how the page go look when dem print am, so e no concern editing suggestions.
hints: List the condition wey you want: make e suggest edits but no delete the original text.
Check whether each option concern document editing, and if e do, whether e preserve the original while showing the changes.

e-h3e-media-d1.explanation: Echo chamber mean group wey dey hear only opinions like their own, so their views dey grow stronger. Chat room wey repeat one message two times na only repetition of sound or text; e no concern bias in opinions.
hints: Echo chamber no mean real room here; na figure of speech. Think wetin the echo stand for online.
Think wetin dey come back again and again like echo, then separate options about sound itself from options about people ideas.

e-h3e-world-1.explanation: Correct answer na language wey people with different mother tongues dey use. The way English dey help people communicate internationally na example. Language wey only one family dey use no fit be common language.
hints: No let the Latin phrase worry you. First compare how each option explain who dey use the language, then cross out options wey put conditions wey too narrow or no make sense.
Compare who dey use the language in each option and how dem relate to each other.

e-h3e-world-2.explanation: Correct answer na stereotype. E mean belief about one whole group wey too simple. Dialect mean the way people speak for one region; e no be belief about people.
hints: For word meaning question, pick the key words. Oversimplified and whole group na the main clues.
First sort the options by whether the word mean idea about a group, way of speaking, event, or family.

e-h3e-world-3.explanation: Correct answer na diversity. Cultural diversity mean different cultures together. Division mean splitting or separation, so e get opposite sense to the description say dem dey live together.
hints: When words get similar spelling, use the explanation after the blank to compare their meanings.
Compare the idea of people from different backgrounds living together with the noun wey fit naturally come after cultural.

e-h3e-world-4.explanation: Correct answer na Their customs are different from ours, and I would like to learn why. E accept the difference and show say the person want learn. Words like strange and backward dey look down on the other culture.
hints: For cultural awareness question, check whether the person dey judge another culture or try to understand am.
Check whether words like all, wrong, and backward dey make general statement or rank cultures.

e-h3e-world-5.explanation: Correct answer na authentic. E mean real and trustworthy. Artificial mean fake or made by people, so na the opposite.
hints: Put the key word genuine from the definition into simpler words.
Think wetin be the opposite of not copied, then first remove the option wey get that opposite meaning.

e-h3e-world-d1.explanation: Indigenous mean something wey belong to the place and the people wey don live there from long ago. Foreign mean something wey come from another country, so na the opposite.
hints: Read the definition, catch the main meaning, then match each word to am one by one.
Focus on the part “the first people who lived in a region.” Find the word about trend, time, or origin wey match this meaning.

e-h3e-write-1.explanation: Correct answer na makes. The fixed collocation “make a case for” mean to give reasons to support something, so e fit the situation where the report dey support a claim with evidence. Does na general verb and e no normally join with “a case for.”
hints: Learn verb and noun pairs (collocations) together, no be only their meanings. Think of the verb wey dey go with “a case.”
Compare the verbs wey dey commonly go with “case” when a report dey present an argument.

e-h3e-write-2.explanation: Correct answer na Organized a school recycling campaign that collected 300 kilograms of paper. E start with a verb and show the work and the result with a number. Helped with various things ... no tell us the actual work wey the person do.
hints: CV suppose show clear results in short form. Avoid vague wording.
Compare whether each option describe a clear activity or only give personal opinion or vague details.

e-h3e-write-3.explanation: Correct answer na Although the museum was crowded, we stayed for three hours. Although show the contrast: e crowded, but we stay long. “So we left after a short time” contradict the fact say we stay long.
hints: Before joining two sentences, first decide the relationship between the facts: cause, contrast, or time.
Think whether the crowded museum and staying for three hours point the same way as you expect or opposite ways.

e-h3e-write-4.explanation: Correct answer na The students who joined the club met every Friday. The subject The students get the main verb met. The option wey start with Because na dependent clause and e no get the result, so the sentence no complete.

For each option, find the main clause verb wey get tense. Check the part after who or because separately.

e-h3e-write-5.explanation: Correct answer na an opinion letter to the board. If the aim na to persuade, an opinion letter wey get evidence and argument fit. Diary entry na personal record; e no be to persuade the school board.

Think who the writer dey address and wetin the writer want from dem, then find the writing format wey fit the purpose.

e-h3e-write-d1.explanation: For the editing stage, you find and correct grammar, spelling, and punctuation mistakes for a finished draft. Gathering ideas na for brainstorming (prewriting), so e different from editing.
hints: Writing stages get order. Think wetin you dey do at planning, drafting, revising, and editing, then choose the explanation wey fit editing.

hints: Use an infinitive after want, hope, and decide; use a gerund (-ing) after enjoy, finish, and mind.

e-m2-inf-3.explanation: After “decide,” use an infinitive: “decided to go” is correct.

e-m2-pass-3.prompt: Choose di sentence wey no correct for grammar.

e-m2-pass-d1.prompt: Choose di correct word for di blank: This bridge ____ in 1990.
